title: Check If a String Contains All Binary Codes of Size K
description: Brute force to optimized: slicing and hashing each substring versus a single rolling bit-hash pass over a fixed-size sliding window.

sections.title: Check If a String Contains All Binary Codes of Size K

content.title: Check If a String Contains All Binary Codes of Size K

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Given a binary string s and an integer k, return true if every possible binary code of length k (there are exactly 2^k of them, from all zeros to all ones) appears as a substring somewhere in s, or false otherwise.

blocks.caption: Slide a fixed-size window of length k, hashing every substring seen

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","A binary string s (containing only '0' and '1'), and an integer k"],["Output","true if all 2^k possible binary codes of length k appear as substrings of s, false otherwise"],["Goal","Check this without materializing and comparing every substring as a separate string"],["Constraints","1 <= s.length <= 5 * 10^5; s[i] is '0' or '1'; 1 <= k <= 20"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["Looking at every FIXED-length substring of a string","A fixed-size sliding window of length k"],["The window's content is a binary string, and there are exactly 2^k distinct possibilities","Represent each window as an integer (its binary value) instead of a string, using a rolling hash"],["A new character enters and the oldest leaves as the window slides by one","Bit-shift the running integer hash left, add the new bit, and mask off the bit that fell out of range"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Given a binary string s and an integer k, determine whether every one of the 2^k possible length-k binary codes appears somewhere in s as a substring.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Combination Lock Checklist
blocks.text: Like checking a very long strip of binary digits to see whether every possible k-digit combination of a lock has appeared somewhere along it, by reading a fixed-size window of k digits at a time and checking off each combination seen, without ever writing out each window as a separate string.

blocks.caption: Roll a binary hash forward one bit at a time instead of re-reading each k-length window from scratch

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Windows of length 2: \"00\",\"01\",\"11\",\"10\",\"01\",\"11\",\"10\" -> distinct codes seen: {00,01,10,11}","All 4 = 2^2 codes found","Every possible 2-bit code (00, 01, 10, 11) appears somewhere in s"],["Answer","true","All 2^2 = 4 possible codes were found as substrings"]]}

blocks.text: Example: s = "0110", k = 1

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Windows of length 1: \"0\",\"1\",\"1\",\"0\" -> distinct codes seen: {0,1}","All 2 = 2^1 codes found","Both possible 1-bit codes (0 and 1) appear in s"],["Answer","true","All 2^1 = 2 possible codes were found as substrings"]]}

blocks.text: Edge case: s is too short to possibly contain every code

There are exactly (s.length - k + 1) windows of length k in s. If this count is smaller than 2^k, it is mathematically impossible for all 2^k codes to appear, so the answer can be immediately false without any scanning.
5. How Should We Think?
Before comparing substrings as strings directly, notice that a length-k binary string is really just an integer written in binary, which suggests representing the whole window as a number.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A binary string of length k directly corresponds to an integer between 0 and 2^k - 1, so there are exactly 2^k possible distinct window values, no more.

Observation 2: Sliding a fixed-size window of length k across s and converting each window to its integer value, then checking how many distinct values appear, answers the question directly.

Observation 3: Converting a window to an integer doesn't require rereading all k characters at every position. A running hash can be updated by shifting it left by one bit, adding the new incoming bit, and masking off the bit that just fell out of the k-wide window.

Observation 4: If the number of possible window positions (s.length - k + 1) is already smaller than 2^k, the answer is immediately false, since not enough distinct windows even exist.

Recognizing that a k-length binary substring is exactly an integer in [0, 2^k) turns a substring-matching problem into an integer-hashing sliding window problem.
This is the fixed-size sliding window pattern combined with a rolling bit-hash, letting each window be represented and compared in O(1) instead of O(k).
6. Brute Force Solution
Slide a fixed-size window across s, adding each window's actual substring to a set, then compare the set's size to 2^k.
Step by step algorithm

items: For every possible starting position of a length-k window, slice out the actual substring and add it to a set.
After scanning the whole string, compare the set's size to 2^k.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Each window is sliced out directly as a substring, since this version does not yet exploit the binary-string-as-integer observation.
A set naturally deduplicates repeated codes, leaving only the distinct ones actually seen.
The final comparison against need (2^k) is the only check needed once every window has been visited.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Every possible window is checked directly by slicing its substring, so the correct answer is always found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n * k), since slicing and hashing each of the roughly n windows costs O(k).
Space: O(n * k) in the worst case, for storing up to n distinct length-k substrings.

Limitation: re-slicing and re-hashing an entire k-length substring at every window position ignores that consecutive windows overlap in all but one character, which can be exploited with a rolling hash instead.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force treats each window as an independent string to slice and hash. Instead, represent each window directly as an integer (its binary value) and maintain it with a rolling hash: shift the current hash left by one bit, OR in the new incoming bit, then mask off any bits beyond the k-wide window. This turns each window update into a handful of O(1) bitwise operations instead of an O(k) substring copy.

Precompute need = 2^k and mask = need - 1. Walk through s once, updating a running integer hash at each character: shift left, add the new bit, then apply the mask to keep only the lowest k bits. Once the hash represents a full k-length window, add it to a set. At the end, compare the set's size to need.
9. Optimized Solution
Roll a bit-hash across s in one pass, collecting distinct k-length window values in a set.
Dry run for s = "00110110", k = 2 (need = 4, mask = 0b11 = 3)

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: seen = {0, 1, 2, 3}, size 4, matching need = 2^2 = 4, so the answer is true.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass over s with O(1) work per character.
Space: O(2^k) for the set of seen hash values, which is at most n as well.
Why This Works

Shifting the running hash left by one bit and adding the new incoming bit correctly builds up the binary value of the growing window; masking with (2^k - 1) discards any bits beyond the k most recent ones, which is exactly equivalent to the oldest character leaving the fixed-size window. Once the hash has processed at least k characters, it holds the exact integer value of the current k-length window.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["i < k - 1","The window is still being filled; the hash isn't added to seen yet"],["i >= k - 1","The hash represents a complete k-length window, added to seen"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: mask = need - 1 (that is, 2^k - 1) is a bit pattern of exactly k ones, used to keep only the lowest k bits of the running hash.
The early length check (s.length < need + k - 1) short-circuits impossible cases before doing any scanning at all.
seen naturally deduplicates repeat window values, since it's a set.

blocks.text: 10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space","Notes"],"rows":[["Brute force (slice + hash each substring)","O(n * k)","O(n * k)","Each window is materialized as an actual substring before hashing"],["Optimized (rolling bit-hash)","O(n)","O(2^k)","Each window transitions to the next via O(1) bit operations, no substring materialization"]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

Recognizing that a binary substring is exactly an integer, and that consecutive windows can be converted between each other via a shift-and-mask update, turns this into a linear-time rolling-hash sliding window problem.
Common mistakes

items: Re-slicing and re-hashing the full k-length substring at every position instead of rolling the hash incrementally.
Forgetting to mask the rolled hash, which lets stale high bits from characters outside the current window leak into the value.
Not handling the case where s is too short to possibly contain all 2^k codes, which can be checked immediately without any scanning.

blocks.text: Edge cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["k = 1","Only 2 codes (\"0\" and \"1\") are needed; the answer is true as long as both digits appear anywhere in s"],["s is exactly the minimum possible length for all codes to fit","Every window must be a distinct code with no repeats for the answer to be true"],["s.length - k + 1 < 2^k","Immediately false, since not enough windows exist to cover every code"]]}

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: State the "binary substring = integer" equivalence explicitly, since it's the key insight that avoids string-based hashing overhead entirely.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Check if every possible binary/fixed-alphabet code of a given length appears as a substring" points toward a fixed-size sliding window with a rolling integer hash, rather than string-based substring hashing.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would this extend to a non-binary alphabet (say, base b)? The same rolling hash works, replacing the shift-by-1-bit with a multiply-by-b, and the mask with a modulo b^k.

What is the largest safe value of k for this integer-hash approach? k must stay small enough that 2^k fits comfortably in the language's integer type (here, up to 20, keeping 2^20 within a plain 32-bit int).
How would you report which code (if any) is missing? Instead of just comparing the set's size to 2^k, iterate over every integer in [0, 2^k) and check for its absence in the seen set.

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Shares its fixed-size sliding window shape with Maximum Average Subarray I, but replaces the running sum with a running integer hash rather than a running numeric total.
The rolling-hash update technique (shift, add, mask) is the same conceptual family as Rabin-Karp string hashing, just specialized to a binary alphabet.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n * k) time, O(n * k) space.
Optimized (rolling bit-hash): O(n) time, O(2^k) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: Fixed-size sliding window with a rolling integer (bit) hash
Core Idea: A length-k binary substring is exactly an integer in [0, 2^k); roll the hash with shift-add-mask instead of re-hashing each window from scratch
Time: O(n)
Space: O(2^k)
Most Important Observation: Binary substrings of fixed length map one-to-one onto integers, letting the window be tracked with O(1) bit operations
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Roll a k-bit hash across s; count distinct values, compare to 2^k
